preamble: The voiced uvular fricative /ʁ/, the usual rhotic of French and German, is deleted in two well-described environments. In colloquial French it drops as the second member of a word-final obstruent-liquid cluster: in 'quatre' and 'autre' the post-obstruent /ʁ/ is lost. This deletion is variable and register-sensitive. It is rare in careful speech, reaches very high rates in casual Parisian French, and is favoured by a following consonant. In German, non-prevocalic /r/ after /a/ is first vocalized to [ɐ̯] and then fully absorbed into the vowel, so that /ar/ and /aːr/ surface as plain [aː]. This absorption is especially characteristic of Standard Austrian German.
phoneticEffects: Lenition, Consonant Deletion, Cluster Simplification, Elision

examples.note: 'quatre' (four): word-final post-obstruent /ʁ/ deleted in casual speech; one of the lexical items most prone to cluster reduction.
'autre' (other): the final /ʁ/ of the /tʁ/ cluster is dropped.
'ministre' (minister): /ʁ/ deleted from the word-final /stʁ/ cluster; Brand & Ernestus (2021) record reductions of this cluster up to [mis].
The vocalized [ɐ̯] of syllable-final /r/ is completely absorbed by the preceding /a, aː/, which leaves no trace of the rhotic.
Wiese (1996) notes a tendency to neutralize [a(ː)], [aɐ̯] and [ɐ]. Under this analysis non-prevocalic /ar/ and /aːr/ become homophonous as [aɐ̯] or [aː].

sources: Brand, S., & Ernestus, M. (2021). Reduction of word-final obstruent-liquid-schwa clusters in Parisian French. Corpus Linguistics and Linguistic Theory, 17(1), 249-285. https://doi.org/10.1515/cllt-2017-0067
